pieces.headline: Sainsbury's agrees £120m sale of Argos to Swift Partners
pieces.one_line: Ex-Co-op boss Richard Pennycook's Swift Partners buys Argos for a fraction of the £1.4bn Sainsbury's paid in 2016, with £70m upfront and £50m deferred over three years.

pieces.headline: High Court rules China's London 'mega-embassy' approval was lawful
pieces.one_line: Judges dismissed a judicial review from Tower Hamlets residents over the 20,000 sq m Royal Mint Court site; the residents' association says it will seek to appeal to the Supreme Court.

bp-north-sea-sale.headline: BP launches formal sale process for North Sea oil and gas business
bp-north-sea-sale.body_md: BP has launched a formal sale process for its UK North Sea business under newly appointed CEO Meg O'Neill, looking to raise roughly £2 billion and accelerate its retreat from the mature region. The divested assets comprise five production hubs generating around 117,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day—about 5% of BP's global output. The proceeds will primarily fund debt reduction as the company reshapes its portfolio. The move highlights the North Sea's diminishing role in global energy supply and demonstrates major operators' steadily shrinking exposure to the region.

boe-gilts-watch.headline: BoE hold stands, but gilt yields push through 5% into August auction
boe-gilts-watch.body_md: The Bank of England held Bank Rate at 3.75% on Thursday, but dissent widened on the Monetary Policy Committee. Three members—Pill, Mann and Greene—voted for a 4% hike, up from two in June. The shift signals mounting rate-hike pressure. The BoE flagged upside inflation risk from Middle East energy prices as a key concern. The September 17 decision will test whether this growing minority consensus translates into a rate rise.

iran-hormuz-watch.headline: Iran watch: strikes weighed, prices rise, Treasury eyes frozen assets
iran-hormuz-watch.body_md:
Reports from CBS News and Times of Israel suggest the US and Israel could decide within days to strike Iranian refineries and power plants, with military operations potentially extending weeks. The reports remain unconfirmed, sourced to anonymous officials.

Iran supplies roughly 3% of global crude oil, plus a larger share of refined products; damage to energy infrastructure would disrupt regional costs and trigger volatility in oil futures. Markets are already pricing the geopolitical premium; watch positioning in energy equities and volatility indices.

chevron-exxon-record-profit.headline: Chevron posts largest-ever quarterly profit as Exxon surges on Hormuz squeeze
chevron-exxon-record-profit.body_md: Chevron and Exxon posted record quarterly profits as refining margins surged on Strait of Hormuz supply disruption. Chevron reported $12.1 billion for Q2 2026, Exxon $14.5 billion—both company records. The earnings surge underscores a critical vulnerability: profitability levels depend entirely on sustained Iran tensions and supply constraints. Should geopolitical conditions normalize, refining margins would compress sharply, creating mean-reversion risk for long energy positions. Earnings-call guidance on margin sustainability will determine whether elevated profits represent a structural shift or a cyclical opportunity exposed to geopolitical normalization.

european-bank-earnings-beat.headline: European and UK bank earnings beat pushes Stoxx 600 to a record
european-bank-earnings-beat.body_md:
European banks reported stronger-than-expected earnings this week, lifting the Stoxx 600 to a record high. Deutsche Bank, UBS, Standard Chartered, and Credit Agricole all beat consensus estimates. Standard Chartered also raised its full-year income guidance, a rarer forward signal this season.

The results reversed sentiment for the banking sector after a difficult year. But the earnings strength may rest on one-time trading gains rather than durable improvement in eurozone credit fundamentals. Standard Chartered's guidance raise offers concrete forward visibility; for the others, the question is whether this season's beats reflect structural recovery or temporary tailwinds driven by sector rotation.

easyjet-profit-plunge.headline: EasyJet profit plunges 70% on Middle East-driven fuel costs, shares hold up
easyjet-profit-plunge.body_md:
EasyJet's third-quarter profit plunged 70%, to £85m from £286m, as jet fuel costs jumped £105m amid the Middle East conflict. The stock rose on the result—a signal that investors have already priced in recovery once fuel costs peak.

Strong forward bookings and holiday revenue indicators convinced the market to look past the quarter's damage. That resilience matters: a 70% earnings collapse that fails to shake a share price usually reflects trader conviction that the shock is temporary and reaching its crest. Fuel volatility remains the critical watch, but the market's message is clear—the acute phase is passing.

ai-chip-rally-record-kospi.headline: Blowout cloud earnings ignite record chip rally from Seoul to Wall Street
ai-chip-rally-record-kospi.body_md: Big Tech's cloud-spending results exceeded expectations in the second quarter, reigniting confidence in artificial-intelligence infrastructure investment after months of investor uncertainty. Amazon and Microsoft reported results strong enough to ease concerns about a potential pullback in AI capex, effectively resetting the narrative for semiconductor stocks. The semiconductor ETF SOXX has advanced 112 per cent year-to-date through August 1st, while SK Hynix and Samsung each posted record single-day gains on the earnings news. The stronger-than-feared cloud results validate chipmaker valuations tied to sustained AI-cycle demand, suggesting the capex supercycle thesis retains significant momentum. Traders will watch whether the momentum extends through summer earnings or falters when forward guidance turns to a slower spending tempo.

burnham-budget-devolution.headline: Burnham government sets 28 October Budget date, unveils mayoral tax-devolution plan
burnham-budget-devolution.body_md: The Burnham government has confirmed an October 28 budget date, with Chancellor Healey pledging to maintain the fiscal rules inherited from Rachel Reeves—resetting market expectations and signalling fiscal orthodoxy will hold despite mounting pressures from social care and defence spending. The constraint caps near-term government spending upside and growth expectations, likely supporting sterling while limiting gilt-yield expansion. Markets had priced in some budget flexibility; the reaffirmation of fiscal discipline may disappoint those betting on discretionary spending before the election cycle turns.

fed-barkin-warsh-meetings.headline: Fed's Barkin calls rate stance a 'close call' as Warsh weighs fewer meetings
fed-barkin-warsh-meetings.body_md: The Federal Reserve is increasingly split over whether its current interest-rate stance is already restrictive enough to cool demand. Richmond Fed President Tom Barkin said the labor market 'doesn't feel tight' and questioned whether further policy restraint is needed, days after three FOMC members dissented in favor of a rate hike. The widening gap between hawks and doves signals potential shifts in forward guidance—a repricing of rate-cut expectations that reshapes outlooks across bonds, equities, and currencies.

proteinmaxxing-formula-prices.headline: 'Proteinmaxxing' trend pushes up UK infant formula prices
proteinmaxxing-formula-prices.body_md: Rising demand from weight-loss drug users seeking to preserve muscle mass has unexpectedly hit infant formula prices, illustrating how trends in one market can ripple through unrelated commodity chains. UK infant formula prices have climbed nearly 5% year-on-year, driven partly by surging wholesale costs for whey protein — a key ingredient in both protein supplements and formula. For traders, it's a reminder that concentrated demand shifts can create friction across fragile commodity networks.

burry-ai-short-bets.headline: Michael Burry expands short bets against Nvidia, Micron, Tesla and SOXX
burry-ai-short-bets.body_md: Michael Burry has expanded short positions against Nvidia, Micron, Tesla, and the Nasdaq-100 index (SOXX), according to recent SEC filings. The contrarian investor is betting that current valuations for AI infrastructure names have outpaced realistic demand. Burry's prescient 2008 housing call lends credibility to his signal, suggesting sophisticated investors may be rotating away from AI bets on valuation grounds. Contrarian investors often prove early, though, so a single position doesn't confirm a turning point—but it's worth watching.

rosebank-jackdaw-consultations.headline: Burnham reopens Rosebank and Jackdaw North Sea consultations
rosebank-jackdaw-consultations.body_md:
The UK government has reopened public consultations on two North Sea oil and gas projects that courts blocked in 2025, signaling a fresh attempt to move energy infrastructure forward despite the risk of another judicial review.

The Rosebank oilfield and Jackdaw gas field consultations launched this week. The government has explicitly acknowledged it expects a second legal challenge—tacitly admitting courts found procedural or substantive flaws in the original process.

The outcome will test whether energy projects can survive re-examination, or whether a second legal loss signals judges willing to block infrastructure repeatedly. At stake: the government's ability to execute policy against opposition, and investor confidence in the sector's viability.

shell-q2-bg-cyprus-sale.headline: Shell beats on Q2 profit, agrees BG Cyprus sale to MOL
shell-q2-bg-cyprus-sale.body_md: Shell posted second-quarter profit of $9.84bn, beating consensus expectations, and agreed to sell its Cyprus operations to Hungary's MOL Group for as much as $720m. The combination reflects a pattern among energy majors: sustaining shareholder returns through commodity cycles while methodically reshaping their asset portfolios. The Cyprus divestiture marks the latest phase in Shell's ongoing capital redeployment strategy. The earnings underscore that major oil companies retain the financial capacity to fund dividends and buybacks while selectively exiting assets they deem misaligned with long-term strategic objectives.

manchester-labour-reform-poll.headline: Labour's Manchester landslide coincides with Reform losing its national poll lead
manchester-labour-reform-poll.body_md: Labour won Greater Manchester's mayoral election by a landslide margin, but the decisive victory came on record-low turnout that complicates any reading of voter mandate. Bev Craig secured 66.3% of the vote against Reform UK's Sian Astley's 33.7%, succeeding Andy Burnham who stepped down from the mayoralty to become Prime Minister. Yet only 25% of eligible voters participated—the lowest turnout recorded for this election—even as Reform has gained ground nationally. The result signals Labour's enduring grip on a major urban centre, but the collapsed turnout raises questions about voter engagement in local politics amid shifting national sentiment.

humala-freed-peru.headline: Peru's ex-president Ollanta Humala freed as corruption sentence overturned
humala-freed-peru.body_md: Peru's Constitutional Court freed ex-president Ollanta Humala on Wednesday, overturning his 15-year money-laundering conviction linked to Odebrecht bribes. The court ruled the conduct wasn't legally defined as money laundering when it occurred, setting him free on a technicality rather than evidence of innocence. The decision unravels one of Latin America's largest corruption prosecutions stemming from the Odebrecht scandal, raising questions about Peru's anti-corruption enforcement and governance stability for regional investors.

ceuta-migrant-surge.headline: Spain's PM blames traffickers as 60,000 migrants cross into Ceuta
ceuta-migrant-surge.body_md: Sixty thousand migrants crossed into Spain's enclave of Ceuta in a single surge—equivalent to roughly 70 percent of the territory's population and a record for the region. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez attributed the influx to trafficking networks spreading misinformation to encourage the crossing; dozens died during the journey. The incident triggered immediate responses across the EU: France and Italy tightened border checks within hours. The crossing exposes vulnerabilities in Mediterranean border controls and signals mounting pressure for a hardline policy shift on migration across the continent.

kyiv-barrage-patriot-retreat.headline: Kyiv barrage kills nine as Trump retreats on Ukraine Patriot pledge
kyiv-barrage-patriot-retreat.body_md:
A Russian overnight barrage struck five districts of the Ukrainian capital on August 1, killing at least nine people and wounding more than twenty as casualty reports continued climbing through the day. The attack—combining missiles and drones against civilian infrastructure—reflects renewed intensity in operations that have persisted into 2026.

For trading readers, significance lies in the downstream effects. Damage to energy infrastructure could lift European natural gas prices higher, while signals of further escalation risk triggering broader equities sell-offs and widening geopolitical risk premiums.

quartz-tariff-quota.headline: Trump signs four-year tariff-rate quota on imported quartz surfaces
quartz-tariff-quota.body_md: The Trump administration will impose a four-year Section 201 tariff-rate quota on imported quartz surfaces, effective August 15, broadening tariff policy into residential consumer goods. The quota on kitchen-countertop and bathroom-vanity materials signals that home-renovation budgets are now targets in the administration's tariff agenda. Building-materials suppliers and home-improvement retailers face near-term margin pressure; the move raises questions about which other consumer categories might be next to face tariff action.

uk-cyber-choices-programme.headline: UK police cyber-prevention scheme diverts at-risk teen hackers from crime
uk-cyber-choices-programme.body_md: UK law enforcement is switching tactics. The National Crime Agency's Cyber Choices programme offers free training to steer at-risk boys and young men away from cybercrime, responding to high-profile infrastructure hacks by teenagers and subsequent jail sentences. The Transport for London and Marks & Spencer breaches highlighted the problem. The intervention-first model reflects official recognition that prosecution alone hasn't slowed recruitment into cybercrime networks—and raises questions about whether early prevention can succeed where enforcement has stalled.

west-bank-settler-violence.headline: UN reports West Bank settler violence against Palestinians at all-time high
west-bank-settler-violence.body_md: Settler violence in the West Bank has reached record levels, according to United Nations monitors, who documented roughly 190 attacks per month in 2026—a 24% increase from the 153 recorded monthly in 2025. The escalation follows a deadly shooting incident near Nablus and represents a significant acceleration in the ongoing conflict. Middle East geopolitical shocks have historically triggered oil price volatility and regional equity repricing, factors financial markets typically reassess as the situation develops.

europe-wildfire-crisis.headline: Europe's wildfire crisis widens: Crete emergency, 300,000+ displaced
europe-wildfire-crisis.body_md: Wildfires across southern Europe have displaced over 300,000 people during the 2026 summer season, with Crete now under a state of emergency after uncontrolled fires forced 8,000 evacuations. The crisis, which has killed at least 23 across Spain and France, marks a scale of climate-driven displacement that typically triggers labor supply shocks and repricing of climate risk across energy and agricultural markets. Investors will be watching whether European policymakers accelerate carbon pricing or infrastructure adaptation spending—policy decisions that will materially reset how climate exposure is priced in the region.

claver-carone-departs.headline: Trump's unofficial Venezuela adviser Claver-Carone departs role
claver-carone-departs.body_md:
Mauricio Claver-Carone, the Trump administration's influential informal adviser on Venezuela policy, has departed his role. Known for advocating strict sanctions against Venezuela, Claver-Carone shaped US policy toward the country, which holds the world's largest proven oil reserves.

His exit creates uncertainty about the administration's strategy on Venezuelan oil and sanctions—a key issue for global energy markets and US oil interests. With his successor unclear, the departure signals potential shifts in Trump-era Latin America policy.

fifa-scraps-investment-plan.headline: FIFA scraps $20bn World Cup investment plan after UEFA boycott threat
fifa-scraps-investment-plan.body_md: FIFA scrapped a $20 billion investment plan for a new events unit after UEFA's boycott vote and public pressure from UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham. The deal, which would have sold roughly 20 percent of the new entity to Kushner-family investors, represented Infantino's bid to shore up the federation's finances ahead of the next World Cup cycle. The collapse signals deep fractures within global football's governance and raises questions about the stability of mega-event broadcasting and sponsorship rights. UEFA's coordination and Burnham's direct intervention demonstrate how coalition pressure can unwind even the largest institutional deals.

mudryk-doping-resolved.headline: Chelsea's Mudryk cleared to play again after doping-ban appeal resolved
mudryk-doping-resolved.body_md: Chelsea's Mykhailo Mudryk has been cleared to play again after the FA and WADA settled his meldonium case, ending a two-year dispute that began with a positive test in 2024. The settlement, which hinged on a procedural change to testing protocols, makes him immediately eligible to compete. The resolution addresses a significant gap in Chelsea's squad, but raises broader questions about the consistency of anti-doping enforcement and whether other pending meldonium cases might follow a similar path.

nhs-puberty-blocker-trial.headline: UK High Court clears NHS-funded puberty blocker trial to proceed
nhs-puberty-blocker-trial.body_md: The High Court has cleared a major NHS trial investigating puberty blockers in transgender adolescents to proceed, rejecting an emergency legal challenge that sought to halt the research. Mr Justice Chamberlain rejected the judicial review bid on approximately 31 July, allowing the PATHWAYS trial to begin around 1 August. The NHS-funded study will enroll approximately 226 children to investigate puberty blockers in adolescent gender dysphoria. The ruling comes despite the Cass Review's recent recommendations for caution. It signals the regulatory and legal appetite to proceed with gender medicine research that previous concerns had cast into question.

eu-ai-act-enforcement.headline: EU AI Act enters full enforcement, GPAI penalty powers activate
eu-ai-act-enforcement.body_md: The European Commission's AI Office gained enforcement powers starting 2 August, armed with authority to levy fines up to 7% of global turnover for non-compliance. From that date, the regulator can penalise creators of large language models and chatbots that fail to meet new transparency requirements—rules applying to any firm offering AI systems to EU users, regardless of domicile. The move establishes the world's first AI governance regime with material financial consequences for major technology companies. How swiftly and forcefully Brussels acts remains unproven.

newcastle-howe-jaissle.headline: Newcastle's Howe resigns as fanbase balks at Jaissle succession
newcastle-howe-jaissle.body_md: Eddie Howe resigned as Newcastle United manager on Friday, ending nearly five years in charge during which the club secured two Champions League qualifications. His departure comes as the fanbase expresses concern over reported succession candidates, with Al Ahli manager Matthias Jaissle emerging as a leading contender. Newcastle will need to identify a replacement capable of sustaining the club's recent progression in European competition following several seasons of substantial squad investment.

massive-attack-singapore-ban.headline: Massive Attack banned from Singapore after Palestinian flag display on stage
massive-attack-singapore-ban.body_md: Two members of British band Massive Attack have been barred from re-entering Singapore after displaying a Palestinian flag during a concert and shouting "Free Palestine." The incident triggered Singapore's foreign-emblem statutes, which broadly restrict political symbols at public events. With no disclosed appeal mechanism and enforcement appearing retroactive, the ban raises questions about compliance unpredictability for international performers and events operating in the region.

china-embassy-ruling.headline: High Court rules China's London 'mega-embassy' approval was lawful
china-embassy-ruling.body_md: UK courts have cleared the way for one of China's largest diplomatic missions outside Beijing. The High Court dismissed residents' legal challenge to the 20,000 sq m Royal Mint Court site in East London, ruling the government's approval lawful. The residents' association is pursuing a further appeal to the Supreme Court, however. The ruling signals London's willingness to advance Chinese diplomatic expansion despite neighbourhood opposition—a modest indicator of bilateral stability even as the legal battle continues.

sainsburys-argos-sale.headline: Sainsbury's agrees £120m sale of Argos to Swift Partners
sainsburys-argos-sale.body_md: Sainsbury's is offloading Argos after a decade-long retail gamble that didn't pay off. The supermarket group has sold the struggling catalogue retailer to Swift Partners—led by former Co-op CEO Richard Pennycook—for £120m, a fraction of the £1.4bn it paid in 2016. The deal marks a strategic retreat as high-street retail fractures under e-commerce pressure and shifting consumer habits. For investors tracking large-cap retail, it's a lesson in M&A miscalculation. Pennycook's turnaround attempt is worth watching: if it fails, it will suggest Argos' woes are structural.

boe-gilts-watch.headline: BoE hold stands, but gilt yields push through 5% into August auction
boe-gilts-watch.body_md:
The Bank of England left Bank Rate unchanged at 3.75% on 30 July, the fifth hold of the year — but the vote behind that stillness is moving. Three members of the Monetary Policy Committee, external member Catherine Mann, chief economist Huw Pill and external member Megan Greene, voted for an immediate quarter-point rise to 4%, one more dissenter than June's split and the largest hawkish bloc since the tightening cycle turned. The headline number didn't move. The committee did.

**In one sentence:** The BoE held at 3.75% but the hawkish dissent grew to three, and gilt yields already above 5% suggest markets are pricing the direction the vote is drifting.

![Bank of England headquarters on Threadneedle Street, London](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/ac/Bank_of_England_Threadneedle_St._%2812565194585%29.jpg)

## A hold with a widening crack

Governor Andrew Bailey framed the decision as a case for patience: UK CPI inflation had fallen to 2.6% in the month before the meeting, undershooting the Bank's own forecast, which he called "encouraging." But patience was not unanimous, and the minutes made plain why. Oil prices have averaged almost 50% above their pre-conflict level in the five months since fighting resumed in the Middle East, and European gas stocks are running below seasonal norms alongside falling global refining output. The Bank's own language put it plainly: risks to energy prices "lie to the upside."

That is the crux of the three dissents. Monetary policy, as Bailey noted, "cannot influence energy prices" — but it can shape how the economy absorbs the shock, and Pill, Mann and Greene judged that absorption is running hot enough to warrant tightening now rather than waiting for confirmation in the data. Bailey pushed back against reading too much into the split, telling reporters there was "no evidence of second-round effects" feeding from energy costs into wages and core prices, and that he could not "draw too much comfort" from the inflation undershoot alone. The next scheduled decision falls on 17 September; there is no Monetary Policy Report attached to that meeting, so the committee will be voting on a partial picture, with the next full forecast round not landing until 5 November.

## The gilt market isn't waiting

While the MPC parses second-round effects, the bond market has already made its own adjustment. Ten-year gilt yields rose 28 basis points across July and closed the month above 5%, a level last breached amid the same Middle East-driven inflation anxiety. Thirty-year yields went further, touching 5.73% — a fresh high in a cycle that has repeatedly tested investors' appetite for long UK duration. The move tracks the same energy-price logic underpinning the hawkish dissents: if oil-driven inflation proves sticky, the path of Bank Rate implied by the futures curve looks too low, and long-dated gilts are repricing to match.

That repricing puts the UK Debt Management Office's 4 August auction under closer scrutiny than usual. Details of the specific gilt on offer were due for release on 1 August, but the timing is pointed regardless of size: the DMO will be testing demand for UK government debt within days of a rate decision at which a third of the MPC voted to hike, and at yields already sitting at levels last seen when the Iran conflict first jolted markets. A soft auction — a wide tail, weak bid-to-cover — would read as confirmation that investors want more compensation for holding gilts through an inflation shock the Bank itself cannot control at source.

## What ties it together

The through-line is that the bond market and the hawkish minority on the MPC are reading the same signal, just via different instruments. Both are pricing an energy-driven inflation risk that sits outside the usual levers of UK monetary policy, and both are arriving at the same conclusion: the balance of risk is shifting toward higher-for-longer, not lower. A 6–3 vote is still a comfortable majority for the doves, but the trajectory — from a narrower split in June to three dissents in July — is the kind of pattern that tends to compress before it breaks. The September 17 decision, made without a fresh Monetary Policy Report to lean on, will show whether Bailey's camp can hold the line or whether the hawks pick up a fourth vote. Between now and then, the 4 August auction offers the more immediate read: whether the market that has already pushed yields through 5% is willing to keep buying at the price it just set.

iran-hormuz-watch.headline: Iran watch: strikes weighed, prices rise, Treasury eyes frozen assets
iran-hormuz-watch.body_md:
The rumor mill on Iran is running hot again, and this time the number that matters is the price of a barrel of oil rather than the number of missiles.

CBS News, citing multiple U.S. sources, and the Times of Israel report that Washington and Israel are weighing a fresh bombing campaign against Iran's energy infrastructure — power plants and refineries — with strikes potentially coming as soon as this weekend. At a Camp David cabinet meeting, President Trump struck an aggressive note: "We'll be hitting them very hard. At some point, they're going to say, 'We just can't take it anymore.'" Asked about reviving diplomacy instead, he replied, "I think we just want to win." One option under discussion, according to officials briefed on the planning, is an intensive campaign running one to two weeks. An Israeli official pushed back on the framing, saying Israel is "unaware of a decision to restart full military operations," nor had it been asked to join. Nothing is confirmed, and nothing is official — but the pattern is familiar. Since Israel and the U.S. killed Iran's supreme leader in a February strike, the conflict has cycled through ceasefires, collapses and re-escalations, with Iran declaring the Strait of Hormuz closed in March and the Revolutionary Guard reportedly hitting two more tankers there on Thursday.

Markets are trading the possibility, not the fact. WTI crude settled at $84.67 a barrel and Brent at $90.12 on Friday, both up more than 1% on the day and part of a roughly 22% climb over the past month. The CBOE Volatility Index pushed toward the 20 level, and one-month implied volatility on oil — a gauge of how violently traders expect prices to swing — spiked as high as 68% last week before easing to 51%. Options desks report demand for out-of-the-money crude calls, a bet that a weekend strike would send prices sharply higher still.

## The bill is already being passed on

That premium isn't just showing up in futures screens. The Wall Street Journal reports that Boston Beer, Sherwin-Williams, International Paper and Unilever have all raised or announced plans to raise prices on beer, paint, packaging and fried-food staples, citing Hormuz-related disruption to shipping and raw-material costs. A Reuters tally since the war began counts 32 companies signalling price increases, 31 warning of a financial hit, and 21 withdrawing or cutting guidance altogether. The framing from executives is uniform: these are temporary, cost-driven increases, not a demand story — but multiplied across beverages, coatings and packaging, it looks less like isolated pricing power and more like a broad-based passthrough that could complicate the Federal Reserve's read on inflation just as it weighs its next move.

## Who pays for the damage

A third thread is quietly hardening from theory into practice. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has directed staff to collect damage estimates from Gulf allies — Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar and Oman — with a view to compensating them for Iranian strikes using Iran's own frozen assets, estimated at $100–120 billion worldwide. One figure circulating puts Gulf damage at $58 billion. Tehran has long called the frozen funds theft and is demanding their return as a condition of any settlement; steering them to Riyadh and Abu Dhabi instead would be one more reason for Iran to stay away from the table.

![Abadan, Iran's historic refinery city and a symbol of the country's oil infrastructure](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/09/Abadan_the_city_of_Oil.jpg)

Taken together, the three threads describe the same trade: a market pricing in a war that keeps almost-ending and almost-escalating, companies passing the cost to consumers before the shooting even resumes, and a U.S. Treasury positioning to make Iran pay for it either way. The next data point is blunt — whether the weekend passes with strikes or without them, and what oil does at Monday's open.

shell-q2-bg-cyprus-sale.headline: Shell beats on Q2 profit, agrees BG Cyprus sale to MOL
shell-q2-bg-cyprus-sale.body_md:
Shell posted a second-quarter net profit of roughly $9.84bn on Thursday, comfortably ahead of the $8.92bn analysts had pencilled in, and followed the announcement two days later with a decision that says as much about the company's next decade as the earnings say about the last three months: it is selling its stake in a Cypriot gas discovery it has held for more than a decade to Hungary's MOL Group for up to $720m.

The two announcements, arriving within days of each other in the final week of July, tell a single story from opposite ends. One shows Shell's current businesses throwing off cash faster than expected. The other shows management deciding, in real time, which businesses get to keep that cash and which get cut loose.

![Shell Centre, the company's London headquarters](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/ac/011_Shell_Centre_-_global_headquarters_of_Shell_plc_oil_company_in_London_UK.jpg)

## A quarter the Middle East made stranger, not weaker

Shell's adjusted earnings of $9.8bn compared with $6.9bn in the first quarter, a jump the company attributed to higher oil and gas prices, stronger refining margins and unusually active trading desks — the last of those a direct product of the volatility that has gripped energy markets since strikes on Iranian and regional infrastructure disrupted flows through the Strait of Hormuz earlier this year. Revenue rose 45% to $94.7bn. Cash flow from operations came in at $21.4bn, and free cash flow at $17.5bn, enough for Shell to cut net debt to $41.8bn from $52.6bn in the first quarter, taking gearing down to 19%.

The segment detail bears out the trading story. Integrated gas, which houses Shell's LNG trading book, delivered adjusted earnings of $2.69bn, up 55% on the year — the business best positioned to profit when regional supply gets jumpy and cargoes get rerouted at short notice. Upstream added $3.49bn and chemicals and products $2.88bn; renewables and energy solutions, by contrast, contributed a token $79m, underlining how far Shell's low-carbon arm still sits from moving the group's overall numbers. Chief executive Wael Sawan called it "very strong results during another quarter of severe disruption in global energy markets," a description that fits Chevron and ExxonMobil's own outsized quarters this earnings season about as well as it fits Shell's.

The board approved a new $3bn share buyback tranche — Shell's nineteenth consecutive quarter of buybacks at that size or larger — plus $1.2bn of deferred repurchases carried over from prior periods, while holding 2026 capital spending guidance at $24bn-$26bn. Shareholder approval for the roughly $10bn all-stock acquisition of Canadian gas producer ARC Resources also cleared this quarter, with completion expected in the third quarter — a reminder that the disciplined-capital-allocation language Shell uses around Cyprus applies just as much to what it's buying as to what it's selling.

## Selling Cyprus to buy conviction elsewhere

The divestment announced Friday hands MOL, the Budapest-based refiner, full ownership of BG Cyprus Limited — a Shell subsidiary whose only real asset is a 35% non-operated interest in Block 12 offshore Cyprus, home to the Aphrodite gas field. Shell will receive up to $720m, made up of an upfront payment plus milestone-linked contingent payments tied to the field's eventual development, with the deal expected to close in early 2027.

![A MOL-branded filling station in Hungary](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/d2/MOL_petrol_station%2C_2018_R%C3%A1ckeve.jpg)

Aphrodite has been a discovery in search of a final investment decision since Noble Energy first found it in 2011. Estimates put the resource at around 104 billion cubic metres of gas equivalent — some 632 million barrels of oil equivalent — but a lack of export infrastructure and disputes over maritime boundaries in the eastern Mediterranean left it stranded for years. That changed on 22 July, when Chevron, which operates the block, secured a fully signed memorandum of understanding with Egypt's state gas company, EGAS, to buy the field's entire output by pipeline under a supply deal expected to run 15 to 20 years. The partners are now working toward a binding agreement and final investment decision, targeted for September, with first gas pencilled in for 2031. NewMed Energy holds the remaining 30% of the block.

In other words, Shell is exiting just as the project's commercial path has become clearer than at any point in its history — which is itself the point management is making. "Our decision to exit is driven by disciplined capital allocation and portfolio choices, as we focus on opportunities that strengthen our integrated LNG value chain," said Cederic Cremers, Shell's integrated gas president. Aphrodite is a non-operated, minority stake in a single offshore field feeding one buyer; it does not touch the liquefaction, shipping and trading network that let Shell's gas division post a 55% earnings jump this quarter. Selling it converts a passive holding into cash for buybacks, debt paydown or the LNG assets Shell does want to run directly — among them the still-undecided second phase of its Canada LNG project, on which the company says it will rule by the end of the year.

## Part of a wider clearout

Shell's move follows a similar logic to BP's decision this year to put its North Sea oil and gas business up for formal sale, and sits inside a broader pattern of the majors trimming legacy or non-core positions even as headline profits hold up — Chevron and Exxon both posted their own outsized quarters this period, helped by the same Hormuz-driven price volatility that lifted Shell's trading arm. The difference is that Shell's Cyprus exit is not a response to weakness; it's a company using a strong balance sheet to walk away from an asset it was never going to operate, in favour of ones it can.

The next marker for how far this reshaping goes is Shell's final investment decision on Canada LNG's second phase, due by year-end, alongside the ARC Resources deal closing in the third quarter — both bigger tests of capital discipline than a $720m Cypriot stake, and both likely to shape how investors read Shell's next set of quarterly numbers.

bp-north-sea-sale.headline: BP launches formal sale process for North Sea oil and gas business
bp-north-sea-sale.body_md:
BP has put its UK North Sea oil and gas business up for sale, a formal step that confirms months of speculation about the company's appetite for one of its oldest production regions. The unit up for grabs comprises five hubs — two in the central North Sea, three west of Shetland, including Clair, the largest oilfield on the UK continental shelf — producing around 117,000 barrels of oil equivalent a day. That is roughly 5% of BP's 2.3 million-barrel global output, extracted from a basin the company has worked for more than six decades.

The process, launched on 31 July, is the clearest marker yet of the direction new chief executive Meg O'Neill intends to take BP: smaller, more concentrated, and considerably less indebted.

![Meg O'Neill, BP's chief executive since April 2026](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/db/Meg_ONeill.jpg)

## What's on the block

BP has not disclosed a valuation or a timetable, but people close to the process, and analysts at Rystad Energy, have put the business at somewhere near £2 billion — a figure consistent with earlier, unsuccessful talks. The Financial Times reported in the spring that BP had held advanced discussions with Ithaca Energy over a near-identical package at a similar price; those talks broke down without a deal. That history suggests £2 billion is less a target than a starting point, and that BP may need to accept a discount, split the portfolio between several buyers, or wait longer than it would like.

The unit employs about 1,100 people. In a statement, O'Neill was careful to separate the commercial logic from any judgment on the North Sea's importance to Britain: "The North Sea remains integral to the UK's energy system. However, as we focus our portfolio and direct capital to our highest-value opportunities, we believe our North Sea business will be better positioned as part of another company." It is the standard language of divestment — not unwanted, just no longer strategic — but it lands differently for a business BP has operated since the 1960s and that still anchors Clair, a field holding an estimated seven billion barrels in place.

## O'Neill's arithmetic

O'Neill, formerly of Woodside Energy and a 23-year Exxon veteran, took over as CEO in April and has moved quickly. BP has since collapsed its three-way divisional structure into two — upstream and downstream — and is working toward $20 billion in disposals by 2027, a bracket that already includes the planned sale of Castrol, the lubricants business. Share buybacks were suspended in February. Net debt stood at $22 billion in the most recent quarter, down from $26 billion a year earlier, against a company target of $14–18 billion by the end of 2027. A £2 billion North Sea sale would not close that gap on its own, but it moves the needle and, more importantly, signals to investors that non-core assets are genuinely for sale rather than merely under review.

![A BP offshore platform in the North Sea](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/28/BP_Ravenspurn_North_offshore_installation.jpg)

The basin itself gives O'Neill additional reason to sell rather than hold. The Energy Profits Levy, extended and raised in November 2024, has pushed the effective tax rate on North Sea production to 78% — among the highest headline rates applied to oil and gas anywhere. Offshore Energies UK, the industry body, estimates the levy will deter roughly £50 billion of investment if left in place. Combined with a moratorium on new exploration licences under the previous government, the basin has become a place for extracting cash from mature fields rather than building new ones — exactly the kind of asset a company chasing debt reduction would rather convert to a lump sum.

## Not the only one leaving

BP is not acting alone. Shell, Equinor and ExxonMobil have each trimmed North Sea exposure in recent years, part of a broader consolidation that has left the basin increasingly the preserve of specialist independents such as Ithaca and Harbour Energy, which has cut more than 600 jobs since 2023 as margins compress. The political backdrop has shifted too: Manchester mayor Andy Burnham's government has reopened consultations on the Rosebank and Jackdaw developments, an olive branch to an industry that spent much of the past two years warning it was being taxed and regulated out of the UK shelf. Whether that shift arrives in time, or with enough force, to change the economics for BP's exiting hubs is an open question — reopening a consultation is not the same as cutting a tax rate.

For BP, the sale is less a verdict on the North Sea's prospects than a statement about its own. O'Neill inherited a company that had spent under her predecessor's climate strategy diluting its oil and gas identity without fully committing to a low-carbon one; her answer so far has been to shrink the portfolio toward the assets that generate the most cash per barrel of capital employed, and sell the rest. The North Sea, taxed at 78% and requiring years of further investment to sustain 117,000 boe/d, does not clear that bar.

The immediate catalyst to watch is who actually bids. Ithaca's failure to close a deal in the spring leaves the field open to Harbour Energy, private-equity-backed independents, or a break-up of the five hubs among several buyers — any of which would test whether £2 billion was ever realistic. BP has given no timetable, which itself says something: a company confident of a quick, full-price sale usually says so.

easyjet-profit-plunge.headline: EasyJet profit plunges 70% on Middle East-driven fuel costs, shares hold up
easyjet-profit-plunge.body_md:
EasyJet told the market on 23 July what most travellers could have guessed from the price of a summer fare: fuel is expensive, and the airline is paying for it. Pre-tax profit for the three months to 30 June fell 70%, to £85m from £286m a year earlier — a number that would, in most other circumstances, have been treated as a profit warning in all but name. Instead, the shares rose.

The arithmetic behind the collapse is straightforward. Fuel costs rose £105m in the quarter to £732m, a 17% increase, as the unhedged portion of easyJet's fuel consumption was bought at prices inflated by the conflict between Israel and Iran. Jet fuel briefly touched around $1,800 a tonne in April, close to the highest levels since the aftermath of Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Cost per seat rose 8% to £85.97, and the airline's load factor — the share of seats filled — slipped 1.3 percentage points to 88.9%, evidence that higher fares and skittish Middle East-linked demand were doing some quiet damage to volumes as well as margins.

![An easyJet Airbus A320 on approach at Edinburgh Airport](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/2e/Edinburgh_easyJet_Airbus_A320_02.JPG)

## A profit halved, a share price unmoved

What makes the release notable is not the size of the fall — airlines have absorbed worse — but the market's shrug. Shares initially rose almost 6% on results day, though that figure needs a caveat: it was recovering ground lost the previous session, when a Reuters report that the European Union might tighten airline-ownership rules knocked 12% off the stock. Strip out that noise and the standalone reaction to a 70% profit miss was closer to neutral than euphoric — but neutral is itself the story. A year in which pre-tax profit fell by five-sixths in a single quarter would normally invite a sharper repricing of the stock. It didn't happen, largely because investors have already concluded that the shock is temporary and close to its peak.

Chief executive Kenton Jarvis framed the quarter as a management job rather than a crisis: the airline said it had "continued to manage the impact of the Middle East conflict, and its effect on fuel prices and booking trends," while pointing to "strong late booking demand for our flights and holidays." That late-booking pattern is doing real work in the numbers. Group revenue actually rose 2%, to £2.98bn, even as costs outran it — the classic shape of a margin squeeze rather than a demand collapse. Jarvis also said the airline was seeing "the load factor gap close for peak summer and an extension of the booking curve," and confirmed fares for July, August and September would run flat year-on-year despite the fuel bill, a pricing discipline analysts read as confidence rather than desperation.

## Holidays carry the group, bookings hold the line

The division doing the heavy lifting is easyJet Holidays, the package-tour arm built to diversify away from pure seat-selling. Its pre-tax profit came in at £84m, down just £2m on last year (and up 7% excluding currency effects), on customer growth of 8%. Hargreaves Lansdown's research note on the update put it plainly: costs are rising faster than revenue can offset them across the group, but the Holidays business is demonstrating what the company calls the resilience of a "capital-light" model — no aircraft to fund, higher margins, and a growth rate now running in double digits. That division alone accounts for more than a third of group profit, a proportion that has crept up with every difficult quarter for the core airline.

Forward indicators gave the market more reason to look through the fuel spike. Fourth-quarter airline bookings stood at 68% of seats sold, only 2 percentage points behind last year, with ticket yields flat — not the pattern of a business managing collapsing demand. Holidays bookings were stronger still, at 87% of capacity. EasyJet left its full-year capacity guidance unchanged, targeting roughly 6% growth in available seat kilometres, and restated its medium-term target of pre-tax profit above £1bn once conditions normalise — a target some way from this year's run rate, with analysts' full-year forecasts clustering around £129m, but one management is not walking back.

![An easyJet Airbus A320 landing at London Gatwick Airport](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/ac/Airbus_A320-214_%E2%80%98G-EZTH%E2%80%99_Easyjet_%2828545202958%29.jpg)

## A takeover battle sitting underneath the numbers

The results also landed inside an unrelated but consequential distraction: a bidding contest for the airline itself. Apollo Global Management has tabled a £5.7bn, £7.15-a-share all-cash offer, trumping a prior £6.90-a-share approach from Castlelake, and easyJet's board has backed the Apollo terms as superior. Both bidders face the same obstacle — EU rules require airlines flying within the bloc to remain majority-owned and controlled by EU nationals — which is why Wednesday's Reuters report of possible tightening on that front did more to the share price in a day than the earnings release did the day after. Castlelake must say by 3 August whether it will proceed or step aside; Apollo's deadline follows on 7 August, a week from this report and a nearer-term catalyst for the stock than any further fuel-price move.

That sequencing matters for reading the market's reaction correctly. Some of the share price resilience around the results is genuine conviction that Middle East-driven fuel costs are peaking rather than compounding; some of it is simply a takeover premium sitting on top of the stock, insulating it from a bad quarter that would otherwise have drawn blood. Untangling the two will get easier once the EU ownership question and the bid deadlines resolve in the coming days — at which point the shares will be trading on fundamentals again, and the fuel bill, not the deal, will decide whether this quarter's optimism was justified.

quartz-tariff-quota.headline: Trump signs four-year tariff-rate quota on imported quartz surfaces
quartz-tariff-quota.body_md:
President Donald Trump signed a proclamation on 31 July establishing a four-year tariff-rate quota on imported quartz surface products, the engineered stone that has become the default material for American kitchen countertops. The measure takes effect at 12:01 a.m. on 15 August, and it marks the tariff fight's clearest move yet from factory inputs into the stuff people actually renovate their homes with.

The action follows a Section 201 safeguard investigation by the U.S. International Trade Commission, triggered by a petition from the Quartz Manufacturing Alliance of America. The ITC found that a surge in imported quartz slabs was a substantial cause of serious injury to domestic producers — the same statutory trigger Trump used for the 2018 washing-machine and solar-panel tariffs. Under the quota, the in-quota duty starts at 25% and the above-quota rate at 40% in year one, both declining by a percentage point annually through year four. Permitted quota volume rises from 140 million square feet in year one to 169 million by year four, allocated on a quarterly basis. Canada, Mexico, Australia, South Korea, Israel, Singapore, the CAFTA-DR bloc and a handful of smaller developing-country suppliers are carved out.

![Engineered quartz countertop installation](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f0/Engineered_quartz_kitchen_countertop_with_waterfall.jpg)

## Who actually pays

Quartz accounts for roughly 36% of U.S. countertop installations, ahead of granite and laminate, which makes this a safeguard measure with a direct line to household renovation budgets. An analysis circulated by the Competitive Enterprise Institute ahead of the ruling estimated the duty could roughly double the material cost embedded in a typical quartz countertop job — from around $504 to $1,036 — and put the aggregate hit across roughly 540,000 annual kitchen projects at $272 million to $559 million. The same analysis put prospective job losses in fabrication and installation at over 6,400, against an estimated 500 gained in domestic quartz manufacturing — a ratio its authors framed as thirteen to one.

The quota is also, in one sense, a mop-up operation. Chinese quartz slabs have carried duties above 200% since 2018, and Commerce imposed anti-dumping and countervailing duties on India and Turkey in 2019 after those countries absorbed the diverted trade. India's exports to the U.S. have since fallen sharply; Brazil, largely on natural quartzite rather than engineered quartz, has picked up share. This proclamation extends coverage to the rest of the field — a broader net than a country-specific dumping case, applied to nearly the entire remaining import base at once.

The next marker is 15 August, when the new rates apply to goods entered for consumption. Fabricators and importers will be watching first-quarter quota allocations for signs of how tightly the volume caps bind; retailers and homebuilders will be watching whether the cost shows up in listed remodel prices before the November data catches it.

fed-barkin-warsh-meetings.headline: Fed's Barkin calls rate stance a 'close call' as Warsh weighs fewer meetings
fed-barkin-warsh-meetings.body_md:
The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady last week for the fifth meeting running, at 3.50%-3.75%. But the vote that produced that outcome — 9 to 3 — was the most openly divided the committee has been in nearly a decade, and the days since have shown just how far apart its members sit.

On one side: three regional presidents, Lorie Logan of Dallas, Beth Hammack of Cleveland and Neel Kashkari of Minneapolis, who dissented in favour of a 25 basis-point hike. It was the first time since September 2016 that three FOMC members broke ranks with a unified hawkish view, and their argument is straightforward — inflation has run above the Fed's 2% target for five straight years, and the current funds rate sits roughly 100 basis points below what a standard Taylor Rule calculation would prescribe.

On the other: Richmond Fed president Tom Barkin, who told the Wall Street Journal it is "a close call whether interest rates are high enough" and that he is "skeptical that the labor market has strengthened meaningfully." Asked directly about employment conditions, Barkin said plainly: "It doesn't feel like a tight labor market." He added that he isn't sure he would have joined the three dissenters, and that "price increases are moving through the economy unevenly" — a hedge, but a telling one from a policymaker who has spent the past year worrying more about jobs than prices.

That split matters because it is playing out just as markets have soured on the man supposed to referee it. Fed chair Kevin Warsh's press conference after Wednesday's decision left investors with no clear signal on the Fed's reaction function, and the reaction was ugly: the S&P 500 fell 1.52%, the 30-year Treasury yield jumped to 5.23% — a 19-year high — and Bank of America's Mark Cabana called it "a classic central-bank credibility shock." PCE inflation currently stands at 4.1%. CME FedWatch pricing now puts roughly 65% odds on a hike at the September meeting, a startling reversal for a central bank that has held rates in place all year.

## Fewer meetings, same argument

Against that backdrop, Bloomberg and the New York Times report that Warsh raised a structural idea at this week's gathering: cutting the FOMC's schedule below its current eight meetings a year. It's a deliberation, not a proposal on paper — Warsh has not stated a preferred number, and he told senators at his April confirmation hearing only that "four is not enough," while declining to say how many would be. He has also floated fewer press conferences and set up five task forces to review the Fed's communications, data practices and balance sheet.

The timing is awkward. A committee this openly split, led by a chair whose own guidance just triggered a bond-market selloff, is an unusual moment to propose giving policymakers fewer chances to speak. Fewer meetings would mean fewer opportunities to resolve — or paper over — disagreements like Barkin's with the dissenters, and less frequent recalibration if incoming data moves quickly in either direction.

The next scheduled test is September, where futures markets are already leaning toward a hike Barkin isn't sure he'd support. Whether Warsh uses that meeting to clarify the Fed's reaction function, or whether the frequency question overshadows it, will say much about which faction is actually setting the tone.

burnham-budget-devolution.headline: Burnham government sets 28 October Budget date, unveils mayoral tax-devolution plan
burnham-budget-devolution.body_md:
Chancellor John Healey confirmed on Thursday that he will deliver his first Budget on 28 October, and paired the date with a pledge that will matter more to bond traders than the date itself: the government intends to keep the fiscal rules it inherited from Rachel Reeves, even as bills for defence and social care pile up on the Treasury's desk. In the same week, Prime Minister Andy Burnham put flesh on his devolution agenda, confirming that regional mayors will get a cut of the income tax raised in their own patches — with the fine print, inconveniently for anyone hoping to model it now, pushed back to the same October date.

Taken together, the two announcements tell a single story about the Burnham government's first real test: whether it can fund an ambitious redistribution of power to the regions without giving markets a reason to doubt its discipline on the public finances.

**In one sentence:** Healey set a 28 October Budget and vowed to hold Reeves' fiscal rules, even as Burnham's mayoral tax-sharing plan adds a new, uncosted claim on the same tight headroom.

## A date, and a promise

![Andy Burnham, Prime Minister of the United Kingdom](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/6b/Official_portrait_of_Andy_Burnham_MP_2026_%28cropped_3x4%29.jpg)

Healey's line was carefully chosen: the Budget, he said, "will be built on fiscal discipline. It will meet our fiscal rules." Treasury officials briefed reporters that the government intends to stay "well within" the two targets Reeves set before Burnham took over from Keir Starmer last month — balancing day-to-day spending against tax revenue by the end of the decade, and getting debt falling as a share of GDP.

The trouble is the room to manoeuvre inside those rules. Reeves left her successor a £22 billion buffer at her last fiscal event, but persistent inflation tied to the Iran conflict has been eating into it, and gilt markets have already registered their unease: the 10-year yield pushed back above 5% on Healey's appointment in July, and the 30-year hit roughly 5.75%, a two-month high. Sterling slipped as investors weighed whether a chancellor drawn from Labour's centre-left, seen by desks such as MUFG as a moderating influence, could actually hold the line against demands from his own cabinet for more defence spending and a fully funded social care settlement. Shadow Chancellor Mel Stride took the opposite tack, arguing the delay to October leaves the country facing "89 more days of unfunded spending commitments and damaging tax speculation."

## The devolution gambit

![Manchester Town Hall](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c4/Manchester_town_hall.jpg)

The policy Burnham chose to headline that same fiscal backdrop is not a spending line so much as a plumbing change: mayors in Greater Manchester, Liverpool City Region, South Yorkshire, Cambridgeshire and Peterborough, and the newer mayoralties covering Greater Essex, Hampshire and the Solent, and Greater Lincolnshire will keep a slice of the income tax and business rates generated in their areas, rather than seeing it all flow to the Treasury and back out through grants.

"More of the taxes raised in a community will stay in that community," Burnham said, framing it as the "biggest transfer of power" of his premiership — notable coming from a former Greater Manchester mayor who spent years lobbying Westminster for exactly this. Healey, standing alongside him, put it more plainly: "For the first time we're giving mayors a share of income tax so communities directly benefit when their economy grows."

The mechanics, though, are still a placeholder. The specific share of revenue each mayor keeps won't appear until the October Budget white paper; an equalisation mechanism is promised to stop poorer regions losing out, and Downing Street has stressed that "the rate of income tax which billpayers face will not change as a direct result of the reforms." Actual cash won't move until spring 2027. The IPPR called the plan "extraordinarily bold"; Conservatives dismissed it as "top-down Manchesterism" of uncertain value outside major cities.

## What the fiscal rules have to absorb

The two stories collide at the Treasury's spreadsheet. Devolving revenue is not, in itself, new spending — Downing Street's insistence that headline tax rates won't move is the tell — but the equalisation payments, the administrative cost of running a dozen new local tax regimes, and the political cost of any mayor complaining about their share all land on the same balance sheet as the defence increase and the social care settlement Burnham has also promised. A government with a shrinking buffer and rising borrowing costs has just added a structurally significant, multi-year commitment to a Budget it swears will still meet the old rules.

That is the bet markets are now pricing: that fiscal orthodoxy holds and the devolution numbers, when they land in October, are calibrated to fit inside it rather than force a rule change or a tax rise to accommodate them. Gilt investors will get an interim read at the August auction; the fuller picture — how much revenue mayors actually get, and how the OBR scores the defence and care commitments against the £22 billion buffer — arrives with the Budget itself on 28 October.

burry-ai-short-bets.headline: Michael Burry expands short bets against Nvidia, Micron, Tesla and SOXX
burry-ai-short-bets.body_md:
Michael Burry, the investor whose 2008 subprime short became Wall Street shorthand for calling the top before anyone else, spent July piling onto a stack of bearish bets against the companies building out artificial intelligence infrastructure. Over a series of disclosures, he expanded existing short positions in Nvidia and Micron, added a fresh short against Tesla, and widened his wager against the semiconductor trade through put options on the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) and, separately, the Invesco QQQ Trust, which tracks the Nasdaq-100 — two distinct vehicles, not one and the same, despite how the trade is often shorthanded.

One thing has changed since Burry's last headline-grabbing call: it isn't arriving via a 13F. He deregistered his hedge fund, Scion Asset Management, with the SEC in November 2025, closing off the quarterly filing requirement that used to make his book public on a two-month lag. He now writes his positions up himself, on a paid Substack called *Cassandra Unchained*, at $39 a month. The market is trusting his own account of his trades rather than a regulatory filing — worth flagging for anyone treating the numbers as audited fact.

![Nvidia's Santa Clara headquarters](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/0f/NVIDIA_Headquarters.jpg)

## The trades

The basket took shape on June 30, when Burry disclosed new shorts in Nvidia, Applied Materials, Caterpillar and SOXX, plus a short against Tesla at $416.22 a share. Caterpillar was a first-time short; he told subscribers the machinery maker's stock had "nearly doubled" on AI-linked capital-spending optimism it hadn't earned. Two days later he shorted Micron outright rather than through options, saying puts had gotten too expensive, with the stock near $1,051.

By late July he had built on all of it: December 2026 Nvidia puts struck in the low $100s, January 2027 QQQ puts struck in the high $500s, and an enlarged Micron short taken near $880 as the stock slid. He also rolled his SOXX puts out to March 2027 and lifted the strikes into the low-to-mid $400s, tracking the ETF's own climb before the pullback.

## Vindication, or just early

The July sell-off has so far rewarded the bet. Tesla fell roughly 24% on the month, closing near $319.69 after a weak earnings report knocked 15% off the stock in a single session. Caterpillar dropped about 16%, to $894.54. CNBC counted four of Burry's five disclosed July trades moving in his favor by month's end.

Burry's stated case, citing the Bank for International Settlements' 2026 annual report, is that a meaningful share of Nvidia's demand isn't coming from end customers at all but from off-balance-sheet financing arrangements among AI infrastructure players — vendor financing and circular deals he argues inflate apparent demand. He has also pointed to the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index's extension above its 200-day moving average, a level he says hasn't been seen since 2000, as a technical echo of the dot-com peak.

None of that proves a turn. Burry's 2008 call made him $100 million personally and his investors more than $700 million, but his more recent record is patchier — he has opened and closed Tesla shorts before, on both sides of the trade. His positions also remain a small counterweight to a market still setting records elsewhere: chip stocks hit fresh highs on blowout cloud earnings even as he was adding to his shorts. The next real test lands with Nvidia's and Micron's upcoming earnings, when actual AI-infrastructure demand — rather than the financing structures behind it — gets measured against the bookings.

proteinmaxxing-formula-prices.headline: 'Proteinmaxxing' trend pushes up UK infant formula prices
proteinmaxxing-formula-prices.body_md:
Britain's supermarket baby aisle has become an unlikely casualty of the Ozempic era. Wholesale prices for whey protein — a workhorse ingredient in both protein shakes and infant formula — have surged over the past year, and the increase is now showing up on receipts for parents who have never touched a protein bar in their lives.

According to Office for National Statistics data, the average price of baby formula rose 4.8% over the year to mid-2026, with a standard 750g box now costing £12.11, up from £11.55. Industry analysts and campaigners trace a good part of that increase back to a dairy ingredient few shoppers think about at all: whey protein concentrate, the powder left over when milk is processed into cheese.

![Whey protein powder](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/9d/Whey_powder.jpg)

## A by-product turned hot commodity

Whey protein concentrate 80 — 80% pure protein, the industrial-grade benchmark — cost €11,733 (£10,050) per tonne in July 2025. By this summer it had reached €25,875, according to dairy market analyst Expana, with some sales of the highest-grade material touching €29,000 and traders bracing for €30,000. Three or four years ago, the same tonne of powder went for under €5,000.

The scale of the move has turned what was once a commodity by-product — whey used to be treated almost as cheese-making waste — into a tightly bid ingredient. "GLP-1 has changed who buys protein, and the whey market is still catching up," one dairy intelligence platform observed, pointing to the millions of new patients on drugs such as Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro who are advised to raise their protein intake to preserve muscle mass while losing fat rapidly. That demand has combined with a broader "protein-first" consumer trend — protein added to everything from breakfast cereal to coffee and Pop-Tarts — to push sports-nutrition buying from a niche market into a mainstream, structural source of demand rather than a seasonal blip.

## Where the formula makers get squeezed

Infant formula manufacturers sit downstream of that same whey market, and they have far less room to substitute or absorb the cost. Whey is used in formula specifically to adjust the protein ratio and improve digestibility so the product more closely resembles breast milk, and there is no easy swap for it.

"Whey is a major ingredient in infant formula, so significant increases in its price risk increasing the price of formula itself," said Dr Vicky Sibson, director of the First Steps Nutrition Trust. Some manufacturers have responded by reformulating recipes to lean on D90 demineralised whey powder, a cheaper alternative that still supplies the required whey-to-casein ratio — but as more producers pile into that substitute, its price has begun climbing too. Jose Saiz, a dairy analyst at Expana, said manufacturers now describe current whey costs as "economically unsustainable at existing retail price levels," a signal that further formula price rises may already be in the pipeline.

The timing is awkward for an industry already under regulatory scrutiny. The UK's Competition and Markets Authority found in its infant formula market study that manufacturers had raised prices by 25% over two years during the cost-of-living crisis, with profit margins running between 50% and 75%. The CMA stopped short of recommending a price or profit cap, and the government's response last December accepted only six of its eleven recommendations. Sibson has pointed to price-cap precedents abroad, including Greece, as evidence that tighter intervention remains an option regulators have simply chosen not to use — which means the whey cost pass-through is landing on a market with essentially no price ceiling to blunt it.

## The wider lesson for commodity watchers

For traders, the interesting part isn't the baby-formula aisle itself but the transmission mechanism. GLP-1 adoption is a pharmaceutical and consumer-health story; whey is a dairy by-product market most people have never priced. The two have collided because whey sits at a genuine bottleneck — it's a fixed co-product of cheese output, not something dairies can simply produce more of on demand — and formula makers, sports-nutrition brands and now a widening tier of "protein-added" packaged food are all bidding for the same limited pool.

That is the pattern worth filing away: a demand shock concentrated in one corner of a supply chain (weight-loss drug users buying protein powder) doesn't stay contained to that corner. It reprices an upstream input shared by an entirely unrelated end market, and the businesses least able to pass on or hedge that cost — formula makers selling to price-sensitive parents under regulatory watch — absorb it last and loudest.

The next data points to watch are the ONS's monthly food inflation release, due in the coming weeks, and Expana's whey benchmark, which will show whether the €25,875 print holds, extends toward €30,000, or eases as cheesemakers respond to the incentive by running more milk through the vat. Any formal government move on formula pricing — a live question since December's partial acceptance of the CMA's recommendations — would also determine how much of this cost increase manufacturers are ultimately allowed to pass through.

humala-freed-peru.headline: Peru's ex-president Ollanta Humala freed as corruption sentence overturned
humala-freed-peru.body_md:
Ollanta Humala walked out of a Lima prison on Friday evening, seven years to the month since the corruption dragnet from Brazil's Odebrecht scandal first swept up a Peruvian head of state. He did not walk out because judges found him innocent. He walked out because Peru's Constitutional Court ruled that what he did — however it is described in the earlier verdict — did not meet the legal definition of money laundering at the time he did it.

That distinction is the whole story. Humala, who governed Peru from 2011 to 2016, and his wife Nadine Heredia were sentenced last year to 15 years each after the National Superior Court found they had funnelled close to $3 million from Odebrecht and, earlier, from the Venezuelan government into Humala's 2006 and 2011 campaigns. It was the first conviction of a Peruvian ex-president to come out of the Odebrecht affair, a scandal so vast — some $788 million in bribes paid across a dozen Latin American countries, and a $3.5 billion settlement with US and Brazilian prosecutors in 2016 — that it eventually touched four Peruvian presidents.

![Ollanta Humala at a military parade in Lima, 2015](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/b9/Ollanta_Humala_en_2015.jpg)

## A technicality, not an acquittal

Humala's lawyers filed a habeas corpus petition arguing that the criminal statute used to convict him did not exist, in the relevant form, when the campaign contributions were made. In a ruling dated 15 July and made public on 31 July, the Constitutional Court agreed, declaring "the entire criminal proceedings against Ollanta Moisés Humala Tasso null and void." Humala left the prison in a vehicle under police escort at around 7:40pm local time.

The ruling does not touch the underlying facts — that Odebrecht and Caracas money moved into Humala's campaigns is not in dispute. It touches only the legal label attached to that conduct, and whether prosecutors could apply it retroactively. Heredia, who ran both campaigns and was convicted alongside her husband, had already sought diplomatic asylum in Brazil last year rather than face prison; it is not yet clear how the ruling affects her case.

## A pattern prosecutors know well

For a judiciary that has spent nearly a decade trying to make Odebrecht convictions stick, this is a familiar kind of setback. Peru has cycled through presidents jailed, prosecuted, or driven to suicide by the same scandal — Alan García shot himself as police arrived to arrest him in 2019 — without landing a conviction that survives appeal. Humala's case was meant to be the one that held. Instead it joins a list of prosecutions unwound on process rather than facts, a pattern that does little to reassure investors weighing how durable anti-corruption enforcement in Peru actually is.

What happens next runs through the same court: prosecutors can appeal the habeas corpus ruling, though Constitutional Court decisions are typically final. The more consequential question is whether Peru's legislature moves to close the retroactivity gap the ruling exposed, or whether the next corruption case now has a ready-made exit.

manchester-labour-reform-poll.headline: Labour's Manchester landslide coincides with Reform losing its national poll lead
manchester-labour-reform-poll.body_md:
Bev Craig stood before a half-empty count hall in Manchester on Thursday night and won by a margin that would, in most democracies, be read as a mandate. She took 66.3% of the vote in the runoff against Reform UK's Sian Astley, who managed 33.7% — a two-to-one drubbing in a contest for one of Britain's most closely watched regional offices. Only one in four eligible voters bothered to cast a ballot.

Both facts are true at once, and neither cancels the other out. That tension is the story: a Labour machine that still knows how to win a fight it chooses to show up for, in a political environment where fewer and fewer voters are showing up at all.

![Manchester Town Hall, seat of the city's civic government](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/7f/Manchester_Town_Hall_from_Lloyd_St.jpg)

## A landslide with an asterisk

Craig, formerly leader of Manchester City Council, was chasing a job made vacant in the strangest way possible: her predecessor, Andy Burnham, left the mayoralty not for retirement or scandal but for 10 Downing Street. Burnham became prime minister on 20 July after Keir Starmer's resignation, triggering the first Greater Manchester mayoral by-election since the post was created in 2017 — and the first time the race has ever gone to a second round.

Under the region's supplementary vote system, Craig led the first round with 47.15% against Astley's 20.99%, short of the outright majority needed to win there. When second preferences from five eliminated candidates were redistributed, Craig's total swelled to 309,525 votes against Astley's 157,178. It took counters fifteen hours to get through it.

What didn't grow was the electorate's appetite for the exercise. Turnout came in at 25%, the lowest since direct elections for the post began — worse than the 34.7% Burnham drew in his last full contest in 2024, and a long way from the sort of participation that lets a winner claim to speak for a city region of three million people. Craig, to her credit, did not pretend otherwise. "For those of you that didn't vote for me, I will still be your mayor," she told supporters. "I'm honoured, I'm humbled, and I stand ready to serve the three million people that live across this fantastic city region."

## The Burnham bounce

The Manchester result did not stay a local story for long. Four days later, two separate polling firms reported that Reform UK had lost its national lead for the first time since March 2025 — a run of dominance that had lasted sixteen months and outlasted a change of Labour leadership.

![Nigel Farage, leader of Reform UK](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/d7/Official_portrait_of_Nigel_Farage_MP_crop_2.jpg)

More in Common's weekly tracker, fielded 24–27 July among 2,061 respondents, put Labour on 28%, up four points on the previous week, with Reform down two points to 24%. The Conservatives held steady on 22%. DeltaPoll, working separately, put Labour and Reform level at 28% apiece. Both pollsters pointed to the same cause: Burnham's arrival in Downing Street, and a first week in office stacked with retail policy — a £2 bus fare cap and a cut to VAT on energy bills among them. "After a jam-packed week of high-profile policy announcements and media appearances, the Labour Party has surged in our weekly poll," said Luke Tryl, UK director at More in Common.

The scale of the swing is worth sitting with. A month earlier, Labour trailed Reform by eight points nationally. Reform's slide comes as Nigel Farage faces his own distractions — his personal finances are under parliamentary scrutiny ahead of an August by-election in Clacton, the seat that first sent him to Westminster.

## Two readings of the same result

It is tempting to fold the Manchester result and the poll swing into a single tidy narrative — Labour resurgent, Reform in retreat — and Downing Street will be tempted to sell it that way. The two data points do reinforce each other: a mayoral landslide in England's second city gave Burnham's first fortnight in office a visible, countable win, and pollsters explicitly credit that momentum, not any single policy, for the national shift.

But a 66-34 win on 25% turnout is not the same instrument as a national poll, and it measures something different. Reform's national polling slide reflects genuine attrition — voters moving from one column to another. Manchester's turnout collapse reflects something closer to disengagement: Labour's core vote held up (or simply outlasted a Reform base that has yet to build the same ground organisation in a Labour-stronghold city), while a large share of the electorate simply stayed home. A council estate turnout crisis is not disproven by a strong topline percentage; it is masked by one.

## What comes next

The two threads reconverge in October. Burnham's government has already set a Budget date of 28 October, alongside a proposed devolution of tax powers to mayors — a policy Craig will now administer rather than merely campaign on. Farage's Clacton by-election in August offers the next real test of whether Reform's national slide is a blip tied to one bad news cycle or the start of a longer erosion. Neither event will resolve the turnout question hanging over Craig's own mandate, which only a fuller local contest — the next scheduled Greater Manchester election — will actually test.
